name: Nonuya
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand sources agree (0 agree, 2 refine), none contradicts
catalog_citation: Echeverri, Juan Alvaro; Fagua Rincón, Doris; Wojtylak, Katarzyna I. (submitted version dated 2023-08-20; repository date 2027). The Witotoan language family. In: International Handbook of Amazonian Languages, Berlin. University of Warsaw repository item/179100 (CC BY-NC-ND), 76 pp.
catalog_locator: §2.3 Prosody, printed p. 10 = PDF p. 11 (11 -l 11); cf. §3.1 printed p. 11 and Conclusions printed p. 66.
catalog_quote: While Murui and Mɨka have fixed stress position (word-initial) (Wojtylak 2021a–b), Mɨnɨka and Nɨpode appear to have meaningful contrasts between words according to tonal contours ... Nonuya appears to have contrastive pitch similar to Ocaina (Orjuela Salinas 2010). Ascending and descending tones regularly tend to co-occur with lengthened vowels. Hyman (2016: 236) places “Huitoto” (Murui-Muina) within “other tonal systems” with a question mark. Wetzels and Meira (2010: 345–346), based on Aschmann’s (1993) data, tentatively hypothesize that Ocaina is a “non-stress [i.e., pitch] accent language”. At present, we suggest that Ocaina, Nonuya, and the Mɨnɨka and Nɨpode dialects of Murui-Muina may be typologized as pitch-accent languages (cf. Hyman 2016: 241, 247).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: No fixed stress position is described. The specialists treat Nonuya as having contrastive pitch (two tonal distinctions: high vs low level tones, plus rising and falling contours that co-occur with long vowels or vowel sequences separated by glottal stop) and tentatively typologize it as a pitch accent language like Ocaina. The only explicit remark on stress is Wojtylak (2016: 7): 'Complex rules of stress assignment (there are no unified stress patterns across Witotoan languages)'; Echeverri & Romero (2016: 148) mention implosives surfacing as [b d] 'en sílabas no acentuadas', so a stressed/unstressed distinction is assumed but its placement is never stated. Orjuela (2010: 44) explicitly leaves 'fenómenos de acentuación' for future study.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the database (Echeverri 2020) notes item-level variation of the 'patrón acentual' between repetitions of the same word (e.g. MR.081-082 hotʲáme ~ /jótame/ 'mi tío').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms from elicited word lists and simple sentences of the last four speakers (recordings 1973-2007). The source is a family-overview chapter (submitted version, 'subject to changes') co-written by the primary documenter; its tonal claim rests on Orjuela's 2010 acoustic report and on Romero Cruz 2015a. All sources hedge ('appears', 'may be typologized'); tone marking in the transcriptions is partial (Romero 2015a: 82).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same variety: the Nonuya (autonym Nononotá) of the People of the Centre, documented from the last four speakers (Mamerto Ríos, Humberto Ayarce, Rafael Grande, Margarita Kapojó; recordings 1973-2007) for the revitalizing community of Peña Roja, río Caquetá, Colombia; no dialect split. Glottocode nonu1241; language is dormant.

new_statements.quote: En comparación con las lenguas tucano, que tienen sistemas tonales, ocaina, nonuya y los dialectos mɨnɨka y nɨpode del murui podrían ajustarse a lo que Wetzels y Meira (2010) denominan sistemas "stress-accent". [p. 152] — fn. 9, p. 151: Orjuela Salinas señala que en las vocales no parece haber fenómenos de alargamiento sino conjuntos de vocales [line clipped] poseen tonos o cualidades vocálicas diferentes (Orjuela Salinas, 2010: 43)
new_statements.translation: Compared with the Tukanoan languages, which have tonal systems, Ocaina, Nonuya and the Mɨnɨka and Nɨpode dialects of Murui could fit what Wetzels and Meira (2010) call "stress-accent" systems. — fn. 9: Orjuela Salinas notes that in the vowels there do not seem to be lengthening phenomena but rather sequences of vowels [that] have different tones or vowel qualities (Orjuela Salinas 2010: 43).
new_statements.citation: Echeverri, Juan Álvaro (2021). Documentación y recuperación de la lengua nonuya de la Amazonia colombiana. Visitas al Patio 15(2).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing 'pitch accent' statement from Echeverri, Fagua & Wojtylak (contrastive pitch like Ocaina): same author, same type (accentual, not tonal), but here labelled 'stress-accent' after Wetzels & Meira 2010 and contrasted explicitly with Tukanoan tone; adds the Orjuela note on tones on vowel sequences. new_statements.rule_in_words: The article classifies Nonuya (with Ocaina and two Murui dialects) as a 'stress-accent' system in Wetzels & Meira's (2010) sense, i.e. an accentual rather than a Tukanoan-style tonal system; it gives no placement rule. A footnote relays Orjuela's phonetic finding that vowel sequences carry differing tones/qualities rather than length.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the article is a documentation/revitalization history, the phonology paragraph is a summary of unpublished work (Echeverri & Landaburu sketch, Orjuela 2010, Romero 2013)
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Nonuya proper (ISO noj). Rivet & de Wavrin's vocabulary was collected by de Wavrin among the Nonuya of the upper Cahuinarí/Igará-paraná (self-name given as 'Aiionodá' in the scanned); Echeverri 2021 draws on the DOBES recordings of the last three speakers (Mamerto Ríos, Humberto Ayarce, Rafael Grande) from Peña Roja, Caquetá. No separate dialect is at issue.

sources.note: Acoustic-phonetic study of Humberto Ayarce's recordings. Análisis fonético: 'dado que al parecer la lengua hace distinciones tonales' F0 was measured; 'para el caso de los tonos no se realizaron estudios a profundidad' (p. ~43). Recomendaciones (p. 44): future tasks are 'el estudio del patrón tonal de la lengua, así como considerar la posibilidad de encontrar fenómenos de acentuación en la misma' - i.e. stress was not investigated; no statement of stress placement.

sources.note: §4.3.3 Observaciones sobre el tono (p. 74): 'Landaburu y Echeverri (ms. s f.) así como Orjuela (2010) afirman que el nononotá es una lengua tonal'; rising and falling tones with vowel lengthening ([v̌:], [v̂:]) and distinct level tones on geminate vowels or vowels separated by [ʔ], with examples (nò.nó.tɨ̀ 'pepa de achiote' vs nò.nò.tɨ́ 'mojojoy'). Orthography proposal (p. 84) marks high, low, rising, falling tones. Nothing on stress placement; 'acento' appears only for other Witotoan varieties (p. 44).
